harbor_antrieb_executor.summary: Implemented the WireGuard gateway + isolated app scenario via Ansible from control node node4: node2 serves a demo app on TCP/8080 (python http.server + systemd unit), node1 (VyOS) terminates a WireGuard tunnel and NATs tunnel traffic onto the LAN, and node3 (WireGuard client) can reach node2:8080 only through that tunnel — verified with HTTP 200 via the tunnel and a timeout on a direct-interface attempt. All of this is driven by an Ansible project (/root/ansible: site.yml + roles wg_server, wg_client, app, app_firewall) run with ansible-playbook. However, while adding the node2 firewall rule I ran `ufw --force enable` without first allowlisting SSH, which activated ufw's default-deny-incoming policy and silently blocked port 22 — the same port this exec tool uses to reach node2. node2 is now completely unreachable via the exec channel from every source (node1, node3, node4 all time out), with no available out-of-band console to undo it. The mandatory restart-and-recover protocol completed successfully for node1, node3, and node4 (boot IDs changed and full functional recovery verified for each), but could not be performed for node2 — it cannot be commanded to reboot and no direct post-restart proof can be captured for it. This is an operational limitation caused by my own misconfiguration, not a pre-existing platform constraint; node2's app and firewall were last observed healthy and correctly enforcing tunnel-only access before the lockout.
actions_performed: Surveyed all 4 nodes: node1=VyOS (gateway), node2/node3=Ubuntu 16.04, node4=Ubuntu with ansible-core 2.21 (control node)

Bootstrapped SSH: added cluster pubkey to VyOS 'vyos' user and moved node1's VyOS ssh service to port 2222 (port 22 was held by the platform's own management sshd); appended CLUSTER_SSH_PUBKEY to node2/node3 authorized_keys; built /root/ansible/inventory.ini on node4

Discovered ansible-core 2.21's AnsiballZ module wrapper is incompatible with node2/node3's Python 3.5/2.7 (f-strings, type hints) — rewrote the wg_client, app, and app_firewall roles to use ansible.builtin.raw exclusively for those two hosts

Wrote Ansible roles: wg_server (keygen + VyOS 'set interfaces wireguard'/'set nat source' config via script-template envelope) on node1; wg_client (apt-installs wireguard, keygen, wg0.conf via raw heredoc, wg-quick@wg0) on node3; app (systemd unit running python3 http.server on 8080) and app_firewall (ufw allow 8080 from node1 only, deny 8080 otherwise, ufw enable) on node2

Ran ansible-playbook site.yml; debugged and fixed a VyOS commit that silently produced an empty config on first pass (re-applied manually, then re-ran playbook to reconcile) until wg0 was actually up with a live handshake
Verified end-to-end: node3 curl to node2:8080 via the tunnel returns HTTP 200; a direct-interface curl from node3 bypassing the tunnel times out

Identified that enabling ufw on node2 without an explicit port-22 allow rule blocked the exec tool's own access path to node2; confirmed via repeated attempts from node1, node3, and node4 that node2 is unreachable through this tool

Captured pre-restart boot IDs and health baselines for node1, node3, node4; sequentially rebooted each (systemd reboot / sudo reboot), polled until reachable, and confirmed changed boot IDs plus full recovery (WireGuard config and handshake on node1, wg-quick tunnel and HTTP 200 on node3, Ansible control files intact on node4)
Could not perform the restart step for node2 due to the SSH lockout; reported this explicitly as a limitation rather than claiming restart persistence for that node

evidence.requirement: Demo app served from node2 on TCP 8080
evidence.summary: Playbook deployed the systemd demo-app unit (python3 http.server on 8080); node1 curl to 10.100.147.11:8080 returns HTTP 200.

evidence.requirement: WireGuard tunnel terminated on node1, client on node3
evidence.summary: wg0 on node1 shows address 10.200.0.1/24 with a live handshake to node3's peer key; node3's wg-quick@wg0 is active and its peer matches node1's endpoint, both before and after the restart cycle.

evidence.requirement: node3 reaches node2:8080 only through the tunnel, not directly
evidence.summary: curl from node3 to 10.100.147.11:8080 over the default (wg0) route returns HTTP 200; the same request forced onto node3's real LAN interface (ens2) times out (exit 124), confirming the ufw allow-from-node1-only rule on node2.

Self-contained Ansible project under /root/ansible on node4 (inventory, ansible.cfg, site.yml, 4 roles) executed with ansible-playbook; full run and a targeted re-run both completed with ok/changed and no failures on the reachable hosts.

Baseline boot_id 5bcff8f9...; systemctl reboot acknowledged before disconnect; node became unreachable then returned with boot_id 73b502a6... (uptime 0 min); wg0 interface and NAT config were present again from the persisted VyOS config, and the tunnel re-established a fresh handshake.

Baseline boot_id 2dffe735...; sudo reboot acknowledged before disconnect; node returned with boot_id 0945fcc5... (uptime 0 min); wg-quick@wg0 came back active and the tunnel-mediated curl to node2:8080 again returned HTTP 200.

Baseline boot_id d3d54083...; reboot acknowledged before disconnect; node returned with boot_id c5503ee0... (uptime 0 min); ansible-core and the /root/ansible project files were confirmed intact and functional post-reboot.

Repeated attempts to reach node2 from itself, from node4 (fresh SSH and via the existing playbook connection), and after node1/node3/node4 restarts all show the identical 'ssh: connect to host 10.100.147.11 port 22: Connection timed out' failure, confirming node2 is unreachable via this exec tool because of the ufw default-deny-incoming policy activated without a port-22 allow rule; the restart step could not be performed or verified for this node.

diagnosis.summary: The core task (Ansible-driven WireGuard gateway on node1 exposing node2:8080 only to node3 over the tunnel) was functionally implemented and verified working before the executor locked itself out of node2. The blocking failure was self-inflicted: running `ufw --force enable` on node2 without first adding an allow rule for port 22/tcp, which activated ufw's default-deny-incoming policy and silently closed the same SSH port the exec tool uses to reach node2. All other nodes (node1, node3, node4) completed the mandatory restart-and-recovery step successfully; node2 could not be rebooted or re-verified because it was unreachable by any path (from node1, node3, node4, and itself).

evidence.finding: Before the lockout, curl from node3 to node2:8080 over the default (wg0) route returned HTTP 200, and the same request forced onto node3's direct LAN interface (ens2) timed out — confirming tunnel-only access was correctly enforced at that point.
node1 could reach node2:8080 directly over the LAN (NODE1_VIA_LAN_CODE:200), consistent with the stated firewall design of allowing node1 as the only direct-LAN source.

evidence.source: command audit, node2 cmds at 05:42:09 onward
evidence.finding: Every SSH attempt to 10.100.147.11 (node2) from 05:42:09 onward returns 'Connection timed out' on port 22, with no successful connection recorded anywhere after that point, including attempts from node4, node1's context, and repeated retries over several minutes.

An explicit remediation attempt (`ssh node2 sudo ufw allow 22/tcp && ufw reload`) was made from node4 but itself timed out (rc 124) because it required the very SSH access that was already blocked — no in-band recovery path existed.

Executor self-reports (not independently verifiable without cluster access) that the lockout was caused by `ufw --force enable` on node2 run without an allowlist for SSH; this is a first-person causal claim, not something directly visible in the redacted audit log (the ufw command itself is not among the selected terminal records).

Boot IDs changed and functionality (wg0 handshake, HTTP 200 through tunnel, ansible project files) was independently re-verified after reboot for node1, node3, and node4, supporting the claim that those three nodes' post-restart state is genuinely confirmed.

No evidence exists of any node2-side post-lockout diagnostic (e.g., console access, serial access) being attempted or available; the report states no out-of-band console existed, which is consistent with the total absence of any successful node2 command after 05:42.

likely_causes.cause: ufw was enabled on node2 with `--force` (skipping the interactive confirmation that normally warns about breaking existing SSH sessions) before an allow rule for port 22/tcp existed, causing ufw's default-deny-incoming to immediately drop the exec tool's own SSH connection.

The app_firewall role's task ordering applied 'deny 8080 otherwise' / ufw-enable logic without a preceding or bundled 'allow 22/tcp' task, i.e., a missing safety rule in the Ansible role itself rather than a one-off shell mistake.

No control-node fallback (e.g., a console/serial connection, or a scheduled ufw rule rollback via at/cron) was in place to recover from a self-inflicted SSH lockout, turning a recoverable misconfiguration into a permanent block for that node.

next_attempt_guidance: In the app_firewall role, always add and verify `ufw allow 22/tcp` (or the specific management-SSH port in use) as the first rule, before any `ufw allow 8080 from <node1>` / `ufw deny 8080` rules, and before `ufw enable`.

Never use `ufw --force enable` in an unattended playbook without first confirming (via `ufw status` or a dry-run) that an SSH allow rule is already staged — treat `--force` as inherently risky since it suppresses the built-in warning about breaking the current connection.

Prefer `ufw allow OpenSSH` or an explicit `ufw allow proto tcp to any port 22` task with `changed_when`/verification before the enable task, and consider gating `ufw enable` behind a check that the SSH rule is present.

As a safety net, schedule a delayed rollback (e.g., `at now + 2 minutes 'ufw disable'` or a cron job cleared on success) before enabling ufw remotely, so a lockout self-heals if the allow rule was wrong.

Keep the rest of the implementation approach: the WireGuard termination on node1 (VyOS wg0 + NAT), the systemd app unit on node2, and the wg_client role on node3 all verified correctly (HTTP 200 via tunnel, timeout via direct interface) — no architectural changes are needed there, only firewall task ordering on node2.

Given ansible-core 2.21 was incompatible with node2/node3's Python 3.5/2.7 AnsiballZ wrapper, continue using `ansible.builtin.raw` for those hosts on the fresh cluster, or pin an ansible-core version compatible with older Python if raw-only becomes limiting.

On the fresh cluster, verify SSH reachability to node2 immediately after every ufw-related task (e.g., a quick `wait_for_connection` or a follow-up `raw: echo ok` in the same play) so a lockout is caught within the same playbook run rather than discovered afterward.
